paper_a.title: Groups of polynomial growth and expanding maps

paper_b.title: A new proof of Gromov's theorem on groups of polynomial growth

metadata.description: Both papers prove the same theorem: a finitely generated group of polynomial growth is virtually nilpotent. Gromov (paper A) introduces metric-space rescaling, Gromov-Hausdorff limits, and Montgomery-Zippin to reduce to a Lie group action. Kleiner (paper B) replaces the limiting machinery with a self-contained finite-dimensionality theorem for spaces of harmonic functions of polynomial growth on the Cayley graph (after Colding-Minicozzi), proved via Poincare inequalities. The two proofs share a common skeleton (induction on degree, building a linear representation, invoking Tits and Wolf-Milnor) but the analytic core is fundamentally different. Paper A is PDF-fallback; matches involving exact LaTeX comparisons are tagged medium confidence.

matches.explanation: Both define polynomial growth of a finitely generated group via the cardinality of word balls being bounded by a polynomial in the radius. Kleiner additionally introduces 'weakly polynomial growth' (using liminf instead of limsup) in the same definition node, which is the slightly stronger setting under which his proof works; the standard polynomial-growth notion is identical.

Gromov makes the word norm and ball explicit as separate definitions; Kleiner folds them implicitly into the polynomial-growth definition via $|B_G(r)|$. Same underlying object (word ball in a Cayley graph), different granularity in extraction.

Gromov defines 'almost nilpotent' (= virtually nilpotent) as a standalone definition; Kleiner inlines the same notion into the conclusion of the main corollary ('virtually nilpotent' = 'has a finite-index nilpotent subgroup'). Same mathematical object.

This is THE shared theorem: a finitely generated group of polynomial growth is virtually nilpotent. Kleiner upgrades the hypothesis from polynomial to weakly polynomial growth, but on the standard polynomial-growth class the statement is identical to Gromov's main theorem.

Both are proofs of Gromov's theorem, but via fundamentally different machinery -- this is the heart of why the pair is an 'alternative proof'. Gromov: build a metric-space limit, get a Lie group via Montgomery-Zippin, construct a homomorphism Gamma' -> L. Kleiner: induct on degree of growth, use Corollary corinfiniterep (built from harmonic functions) to get an infinite linear image, then close out via Tits/Wolf-Milnor and Wilkie's lemma. The high-level induction-on-growth schema is the same, but the construction of the linear representation is wholly different.

Cluster correspondence: in each proof there is a 'finite-dimensional object on which Gamma acts' that is the analytic engine of the argument. Gromov builds it via Gromov-Hausdorff convergence of rescaled groups (DP396.9-12, LP396.8-9, CP396.4) producing a finite-dimensional Lie-group-acting limit space (TP396.10). Kleiner replaces this entire apparatus with the finite-dimensionality of harmonic functions of polynomial growth (TP397.1, technical version TP397.3 with proof PP397.6). Both yield a finite-dimensional G-equivariant object that drives the eventual representation.

Both papers extract a finite-dimensional linear representation of G with infinite image as the key bridge from analysis to algebra. Gromov: 'algebraic lemma' (LP396.4) plus its corollary (CP396.3) state that arbitrarily-large-image homomorphisms into a Lie group force virtual nilpotence under polynomial growth. Kleiner: corollary corinfiniterep (CP397.1) directly produces an infinite linear representation, with PP397.7 the explicit construction via harmonic maps and Property (T) failure. Same role in the proof; very different sources.

Gromov's splitting lemma: an infinite-index subgroup of G has growth at most growth(G) - 1. Kleiner uses Wilkie's lemma in PSP397.28 to bound the degree of the kernel K of G -> Z by deg(G) - 1 in the inductive step. Both lemmas serve the same purpose -- providing an inductive descent of the growth/degree -- and have nearly identical statements; the underlying combinatorial idea is the same.

Both choose 'good scales' at which the volume function obeys controlled doubling-type inequalities: Gromov's i-regular radii (DP396.13) and Kleiner's selection of scales i_1, i_2 (LP397.1). They serve as the discrete-rescaling backbone of each proof -- selecting radii where polynomial growth gives uniform control. Different formulations (radii indexed by power-of-2 vs power-of-16; condition on log b vs log V) but the same idea: pigeonhole the doubling at carefully chosen scales.

Both prove the existence of arbitrarily many good scales by a pigeonhole / contradiction argument against polynomial growth. Gromov's regularity lemma (LP396.3) constructs an i-regular sequence; Kleiner's proof PP397.2 of the good-scales lemma uses essentially the same telescoping argument.

Both papers establish a foundational inequality on group balls used to control growth. Gromov's covering inequality b(2r) <= b(4r)/b(r) (EP396.2) is a discrete combinatorial doubling-type bound. Kleiner's Poincare inequality (TP397.2 / EP397.1) is a functional-analytic L^2-Poincare inequality on Cayley graphs. Both serve as the 'fundamental local control' on Cayley balls, but they capture quite different phenomena -- one is purely combinatorial, the other involves gradients.

Both proofs cite the Milnor-Wolf theorem (solvable + polynomial growth => virtually nilpotent) as a final-stage closing argument. Gromov's TP396.5 is the explicit external citation; Kleiner invokes Wolf-Milnor inside PSP397.27 (and again at the end of PSP397.29). Same external result, used in the same role.

Both proofs cite Tits' alternative for finitely generated linear groups -- Gromov as TP396.6, Kleiner inside PSP397.27 ('Tits' alternative (or Shalom)') -- to deduce that an infinite linear image is virtually solvable. Same external theorem, identical role.

Jordan's theorem on finite subgroups of Lie groups appears in Gromov's algebraic lemma machinery (via LP396.5) but does not feature in Kleiner's argument, which avoids the Lie-group-of-isometries step entirely.

Montgomery-Zippin (TP396.8) is the key external input to Gromov's proof: it converts the homogeneous metric limit into a Lie group acting transitively. Kleiner's proof eliminates this step entirely -- harmonic-function methods replace the Lie-group reduction. This is the most distinctive Gromov-only ingredient.

The Svarc-Milnor relation between fundamental-group growth and universal-cover volume growth, together with its corollary, is part of Gromov's 'expanding maps' application context (CP396.1, ProbP396.1). It has no analogue in Kleiner's proof, which is strictly group-theoretic and does not pass through Riemannian universal covers.
The 'totally expanding => polynomial growth' lemma underlies Gromov's expanding-maps application (Franks' theorem). Kleiner does not consider expanding maps.

Gromov's auxiliary Lemma (b) -- the commutator subgroup of a polynomial-growth group is finitely generated -- is a delicate combinatorial result tied to his algebraic-lemma argument. Kleiner's proof routes around the need for this fact entirely.

Auxiliary Lemma (a) -- existence of finite-index subgroup with infinite-index commutator under bounded-image hypotheses -- is internal scaffolding for Gromov's algebraic lemma; Kleiner's proof structure does not require it.

Gromov's 'localization lemma' lives in the Lie-group-of-isometries machinery and produces small-displacement isometries with arbitrarily large generated subgroups. Kleiner avoids isometric actions on metric limits, so this lemma has no counterpart.

The displacement lemma (LP396.10) tunes conjugates so the rescaled displacement converges to a prescribed value; this is a hallmark of Gromov's metric-limit approach. Kleiner has no use for displacement-on-metric-limit machinery.

Gromov's geometric corollary (an expanding self-map of a compact manifold is conjugate to an infra-nil-endomorphism) and the associated classification problem are application-level consequences of the main theorem in the dynamical-systems setting. Kleiner's paper has no analogous application -- it is a focused replacement of Gromov's proof, not the surrounding context.

Gromov's effective version (polynomial-growth control on a finite range R already forces virtual nilpotence) and the related open problem on the dependence of constants. Kleiner's paper does not address effective bounds.
Geometric application to Ricci-bounded Riemannian manifolds with small-displacement isometries. Outside Kleiner's scope.

Definitions tied to Gromov's expanding-maps application (expanding map, infra-nil-manifold, topological conjugacy, geometric growth on a Riemannian manifold). Kleiner's paper does not engage with this material.
Displacement function D(gamma, r) is internal scaffolding for Gromov's PP396.9; Kleiner's proof flow does not introduce a comparable object.
f-length and polynomial f-growth on a filtered nilpotent group -- internal to Tits' Appendix A1 (Bass-Wolf computation of growth degree of a nilpotent group). No counterpart in Kleiner.
Bass-Wolf precise polynomial-growth degree formula d = sum i d_i for nilpotent groups (Tits' appendix). Independent contribution of Tits's appendix; not in Kleiner's paper.

Tits' Lemmas 1-3 (short-word bound for central elements; Z-extension of nilpotent kernels; spectral lemma on automorphisms of free abelian groups). All belong to Tits' appendix and have no analogue in Kleiner.
Geometric infinite-version of the main theorem (torsion-free with bounded-growth subgroups) using Auslander-Schenkman. Outside Kleiner's scope.
Effective dependence of Gromov's constants on d, k -- open problem stated by Gromov; not addressed by Kleiner.

Kleiner's 'degree of growth' deg(G) = min{d in N : liminf V(r)/r^d < infinity} is the integer parameter on which his induction is run. Gromov uses the (real) growth degree implicitly but does not formalize this minimal-integer notion; the framing is specific to Kleiner's argument.
Definition of harmonic map on a Cayley graph (graph -> Hilbert space). Central to Kleiner's analytic core; entirely absent from Gromov's metric-limit proof.

Properties of the controlled cover B (multiplicity bound, cardinality |J| < e^{wa}, local Poincare on cover balls) and its proof. Internal to Kleiner's harmonic-function machinery; no Gromov counterpart.
The harmonic vs non-harmonic two-term bound via Phi (LP397.3), its proof (PP397.4), and the Schoen-Yau reverse Poincare (EP397.2). Heart of Kleiner's analytic argument; no analogue in Gromov.

Selection of the controlled-growth subspace U (half-dimensional subspace on which Q_{16R_2} <= e^{2a} Q_{R_2}) and its proof via simultaneous diagonalization of quadratic forms. Internal to Kleiner; no Gromov analogue.

Kleiner's Appendix A: Property (T) framework -- its definition, equivalent characterizations (Fisher-Margulis weak version), the harmonic-map-existence criterion, energy function, and energy critical-point characterization. This whole apparatus produces the G-equivariant harmonic map used in PP397.7 and is wholly absent from Gromov's argument.

Kleiner's proof of the Poincare inequality (TP397.2) via Cauchy-Schwarz along shortest paths and a multiplicity bound on the path map. Bespoke to the harmonic-function framework; no parallel in Gromov.
